headline_marked: Developer builds proxy to [[force LLMs to answer]] any prompt, bypassing refusals
headline: Developer builds proxy to force LLMs to answer any prompt, bypassing refusals
summary: Tired of AI refusals? This self-hosted gateway retries prompts with 62 mutation operators until a usable answer is returned.
details: Developers working with LLM APIs often encounter frustrating refusals, where the AI provides lectures or disclaimers instead of direct answers. To combat this, a developer has created armor-gw, an OpenAI-compatible proxy designed to intercept and retry prompts until a satisfactory response is obtained.

The armor-gw proxy inspects every response using 13 detector classes to identify not only explicit refusals but also subtle evasions. When a refusal is detected, the request is reformulated using one of 62 mutation operators and retried. A second variant generated by a different strategy family runs in parallel, ensuring the fastest valid answer is delivered.

The system employs a Thompson-sampling bandit strategy layer that learns which approach—persona framing, encoding tricks, or inversion techniques—works best for specific models. A diagnostic judge categorizes refusals by cause (policy, safety-speak, capability doubt, evasion) to inform subsequent retry attempts.

Key features include support for multiple upstreams, per-model routing, and failover capabilities. The console UI provides a live view of the retry process, making it engaging to watch the gateway classify refusals and overcome them.

Detecting refusals is challenging, as keyword lists are easily bypassed. The most reliable signal identified is the entity survival rate: if technical nouns from the original request are absent in the response, the question was not answered.
The gateway also focuses on output hygiene, stripping chain-of-thought leaks, disclaimers, filler questions, and unnecessary conversational elements to deliver a clean, direct answer.
A regression bank with 65 seeded test cases runs on demand to flag any topic whose success rate drops by more than 20%, ensuring the system adapts to upstream model updates.
armor-gw is self-hosted, released under the MIT license, and features a one-command deployment. It requires Python 3.9+ and can run on minimal hardware, including ARM-based systems.
